dek: The court in plain English, four rules that get you playing, the starter paddle set and bottle worth bringing, and what to say when you walk up to a game.

body.text: Racket, paddle or a very small tennis shoe? If you've heard 'pickleball' a hundred times and still couldn't say what you hit the ball with, here's the whole picture in a few minutes: a paddle, a ball and a short list of rules, and by the end of your first session you could be playing. It's one of the more forgiving sports to walk into as a beginner: the court is small and the pace is manageable.

Pickleball is a paddle sport played over a low net on a small court, most often as doubles. It borrows from tennis, badminton and table tennis. You hit a light, perforated plastic ball with a solid paddle, not a stringed racket. Because the court is compact, there's less ground to cover, and open play tends to rotate partners, so it's an easy sport to be bad at in good company.
What to bring, and what to skip

essentials: A paddle, or a starter set that bundles paddles and balls
A few pickleballs; per the official rulebook, approved balls are fine indoors or outdoors, so one kind covers you
Shoes with good grip that will not mark the court
optional: A starter set that bundles paddles and balls, handy if you're playing with a friend
A small tote for balls, water and a spare layer
Court shoes made for racquet sports, as a later upgrade
A better paddle once you've played enough to know what you like

body.text: You probably own the shoes and a water bottle already; a bottle you love is easy to keep courtside. A starter set bundles paddles and balls, which is handy for playing with a friend, and your own paddle means you can play whenever a friend texts. Some clubs and beginner sessions lend paddles if you'd like to try one first. For casual play nobody is checking your paddle; if you ever plan to compete, look at your national governing body's equipment guidance first. A better paddle can come later, once you know whether you like a lighter feel or something with more punch.
**What makes it easier:** a starter set with two paddles and balls, so you and a friend can play the same afternoon you decide to.

body.title: Your first pickleball kit
body.dek: A starter set bundles paddles and balls, so you and a friend can play whenever the mood strikes. Add a water bottle and a tote for the court bag.

body.text: The court is 20 feet by 44 feet, with a low net: 36 inches at the sidelines and 34 inches in the middle. Close to the net on each side, 7 feet out, is a marked zone nicknamed 'the kitchen' (officially the non-volley zone). It's the part that trips up almost every beginner, because in general you aren't allowed to hit the ball out of the air while you're standing in it. You can step in to play a ball that has already bounced. Ask whoever you're playing with to point out the lines on your first day.

items: **Serve underhand,** diagonally across the court and past the kitchen. Ask a friendly player to show you the box.
**Let it bounce twice.** After the serve, the ball has to bounce once on each side before anyone can volley. It keeps rallies alive.
**Mind the kitchen** when volleying, as above.

**Say the score out loud.** Most games are played to eleven, winning by two, and in traditional scoring only the serving side scores. Calling the score before each serve keeps everyone on the same page.

body.text: That's enough to play. If a rule confuses you, ask. People who love this game are usually delighted to explain it.
A first session that doesn't ask much

steps: Walk, loosen your shoulders and swing your arms a little.
Rally softly with a partner from just behind the kitchen line, counting how many hits you can string together.
Practice ten underhand serves into the correct diagonal.
Play a relaxed game with the double-bounce rule and forget the score.
Cool down, drink water and stop if anything hurts.

body.text: **Worth bringing:** a small tote for balls, water and a spare layer, so the whole session fits in one bag.

items: **Swinging too hard.** Placement and patience go a long way.
**Forgetting the double bounce.** A quiet reminder before each serve fixes it.
**Playing through pain.** If your shoulder or wrist aches, rest, and see a doctor if it lingers.

body.title: For the second month
body.dek: Court shoes made for racquet sports and a tote that carries the lot, once you know you're hooked.

body.text: The easiest route is a friend, plus a second friend to make four. Many public courts run open play, with a sign-in or paddle-stacking system that varies from court to court, and your local recreation department may run beginner clinics. Arrive early, watch for ten minutes to see how people rotate, then say, 'Hi, I'm new. Can I join the next game?' Open play often mixes levels, which is a friendly way to learn. Call lines fairly on your own side of the net, meet at the net after a game, and check how the paddle rack works on each court, since it varies.
Who is your first rally partner? Two people are plenty for a first session, and four make a proper doubles game.
